blocks.text: [II, 708] I shall now say why I think that ברברים אבוסים are neither fattened hens, nor guinea fowl, nor birds in general. 1. Although among the later Hebrews [col. 135] אבס abas is said also of birds that are fattened, yet in Scripture אבוס ebus is the manger of cattle or beasts of burden, not a fattening coop for birds. And אבס abas, derived from it, is applied only to cattle. Hence, when those who had come with Cadmus occupied the island of Euboea, as is found in Strabo, their leader was called אבס Abas, that is, fattener of cattle. From this, with a Greek inflection, the inhabitants themselves were called Abantes ^{(3)}. For the greatest Poet calls them by no other name. So too the island was called Εὔβοια [Euboia] from oxen, and Ἀργιβόειος [Argiboeios] in Aelian, book 12, chapter 36. For that this island was long ago famous for its ox pastures is shown by the oxen driven off from Euboea by Autolycus, of which Apollodorus speaks in book 2 of the Bibliotheca, and Tzetzes, Chil. 8. Accordingly, at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War the Athenians πρόβατα, καὶ ὑποζύγια εἰς τὴν Εὔβοιαν διεπέμψαντο [probata, kai hypozygia eis tēn Euboian diepempsanto], sent their sheep and beasts of burden to Euboea, as Thucydides has it in book 2; and on the coinage of the Euboeans an ox's head was engraved. So Antonius Augustinus testifies in Dialogue 3 On Coins. But on Euboea see more in our Chanaan. 2. If by ברברים אבוסים the Sacred Writer meant to signify birds, of which there had been no mention before, there appears no reason why, content with epithets alone, he did not expressly name צפורים, that is, birds, so that there would be no room for doubt. 3. The same objection can be raised regarding the gallinaceous kind. For no one would say that ברברים are cocks or hens. 4. If the ברבורים had their name from Barbary, they would not be called barburim, but barbarim. 5. And although the eastern coast of Africa long ago bore the name of Barbary, yet that this was already in use in the age of Solomon cannot be proved by any argument. 6. Finally, who would believe that guinea fowl, or birds of Barbary, whatever they may have been, came into the reckoning of Solomon's provisions rather than so many others native to Judaea and the neighbouring regions, which were set daily on the royal table? 7. But there was no need to descend so far. Otherwise fish too, and vegetables, and the fruits of trees, and every kind of delicacy ought to have been listed together. Josephus saw this in part. And so he added fish to the birds on his own account. Ταῦτα πάντα, he says, πάρεξ τῶν ἐπ᾽ ἄγρας ἐλάφων λέγω, καὶ βουβάλων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν, καὶ ἰχθύων, ἐκομίζετο καθ᾽ ἡμέραν τῷ βασιλεῖ· [Tauta panta, parex tōn ep᾽ agras elaphōn legō, kai boubalōn, kai tōn ptēnōn, kai ichthyōn, ekomizeto kath᾽ hēmeran tō basilei] All these, besides wild animals taken in the hunt, I mean deer and bubali, and birds, and fish, were brought daily to the king, book 8, ch. 2 Antiqu.
